name: Netherlands
title: The Netherlands: tuition, application fees and the scholarships that cover them
meta_title: Netherlands tuition fees for international students, by university
lede: Dutch universities teach hundreds of programmes in English. Students from outside the EU/EEA pay institutional fees: from about €9,300 a year at universities of applied sciences, and mostly €18,000–€26,000 for a research-university master's. The funded routes are university scholarships such as TU Delft's Van Effen and Maastricht's NL-High Potential.
description: Non-EU tuition at each Dutch research university and 11 universities of applied sciences for 2026–27, the cheapest from €9,314, and the €100 application fee.

sections.html: EU/EEA students pay the Dutch statutory fee (€2,694 for 2026–27). Students from outside the EU/EEA pay an institutional fee set by each university: for a master's, mostly between about €18,000 and €26,000 a year, and up to about €37,000 for medicine and dentistry.

sections.h: Tuition fees at each Dutch university
sections.html:
These are the yearly institutional fees for full-time students from outside the EU/EEA, as each research university publishes them. Fees go up every year, usually by about 3%, so check the year column: TU Delft's MSc fee is €25,633 for 2026–27 and €26,479 for 2027–28. TU Eindhoven's bachelor's fee rises more, from €18,600 to €22,400.

A dash means the fee is set programme by programme; the programme's own page on the university's site gives the exact amount. Other 2027–28 rates already published: Utrecht's master's fees run from €22,000 to €33,500, Twente's are €18,720 or €22,320, Eindhoven's master's fee is €22,400, and Groningen's bachelor's fees start at €14,400.

sections.h: Universities of applied sciences: the lower-cost route
sections.html:
Universities of applied sciences (hogescholen) teach practice-based bachelor's degrees, and some master's, in English. They charge non-EU students far less than research universities: about €9,300 to €10,700 a year at most of them for 2026–27, against €13,200 to €34,500 for a bachelor's at a research university. These are the institutional fees each school publishes for students from outside the EU/EEA, cheapest first.

sections.h: Application fees, and the Dutch universities that charge none
sections.html:
Almost every Dutch research university charges €100 to applicants whose previous degree is from outside the Netherlands. It is not refunded if you are turned down, and the university will not assess your file until it has been paid.

So the Dutch universities you can apply to without losing money are Wageningen, Twente for master's programmes outside those three faculties, and Maastricht, which gives the fee back when you enrol. Among universities of applied sciences, Saxion's cost table lists no application fee either. See also our guide to universities with no application fee in other countries.

The lowest non-EU fees in the Netherlands are at universities of applied sciences. For a 2026–27 bachelor's, Windesheim (€9,314), HAN (€9,320 for Communication, International Business and International Social Work), Saxion (€9,360), HZ (€9,893) and Van Hall Larenstein (€9,950) charge least, and Van Hall Larenstein's International Agribusiness and Trade costs €8,830.

Among research universities, the lowest non-EU master's fees for 2026–27 are at the University of Twente (€18,200 for its lower-rate programmes), Groningen (€19,900 in arts, philosophy and religion) and Tilburg (€19,900). For a bachelor's, Maastricht (from €13,200), Tilburg (€13,400), Utrecht (from €13,415) and Erasmus (€13,500) cost least. Wageningen charges non-EU master's students €21,900 for 2026–27, with €22,500 expected for 2027–28.

The only way to study in the Netherlands for nothing is a full scholarship, such as the two below.

Two routes on this board cover tuition and living costs:

  • TU Delft's Justus & Louise van Effen Excellence Scholarship: about 16 awards across two-year MSc programmes; apply with a complete MSc application by 1 December.
  • Maastricht University's NL-High Potential Scholarship: 18 awards for 2027–28 covering tuition, living expenses (€20,150 for a 13-month programme), insurance and visa costs; master's application by 10 December, scholarship by 1 February.

Dutch scholarship deadlines fall months before regular admission deadlines, and you normally need a complete admission application first. For a September start, have your transcripts, English test and references ready by November of the previous year.
Student housing is scarce in Delft, Amsterdam, Utrecht and other university cities. Look as soon as you are admitted, and be wary of listings that ask for payment before you have seen a contract.

sections.h: Proof of funds for your residence permit
sections.html: The Dutch immigration service (IND) asks you to show the study norm: €1,130.77 a month for university and higher professional education in 2026, the most a Dutch student can receive in study finance when living away from home. You need it for a year (twelve times the monthly amount, €13,569.24), and in practice you usually transfer it to your university, which applies for the permit for you. The amount changes every 1 January.

You may work as an employee only if your employer has a work permit (TWV) for you, and then you must choose: up to 16 hours a week, or full time in June, July and August. Self-employment does not need a work permit, as long as you still meet the conditions of your study permit.

sections.h: After you graduate: the orientation year
sections.html: Within three years of finishing your studies, you can apply for a residence permit for an orientation year for highly educated persons. It lasts one year, and during it you may work freely: your employer does not need a work permit.

faq.q: Which universities in the Netherlands have no application fee?
faq.a: Wageningen University lists no application fee. Maastricht University charges €100 but refunds it once you start your studies, and at the University of Twente only master's programmes in three faculties charge it. The other research universities charge €100 to applicants with a non-Dutch degree.

faq.q: How much are tuition fees in the Netherlands for international students?
faq.a: Students from outside the EU/EEA pay an institutional fee set by each school. At universities of applied sciences it is about €9,300 to €10,700 a year for most 2026–27 bachelor's programmes. At research universities a master's costs mostly €18,000 to €26,000 a year, and up to about €37,000 for medicine and dentistry; the cheapest start at €18,200 at Twente and €19,900 at Groningen and Tilburg.

faq.q: Which are the cheapest universities in the Netherlands for international students?
faq.a: Universities of applied sciences: for a 2026–27 bachelor's, Windesheim charges non-EU students €9,314, HAN from €9,320, Saxion €9,360 and HZ €9,893. Among research universities, Twente, Groningen and Tilburg have the lowest master's fees. A full scholarship such as TU Delft's Van Effen or Maastricht's NL-High Potential covers tuition and living costs.

faq.q: How much money do I need for a Dutch student residence permit?
faq.a: The 2026 study norm for university and higher professional education is €1,130.77 a month, and you need it for a year: €13,569.24.

faq.q: Can I work while studying in the Netherlands?
faq.a: Only if your employer gets a work permit for you, and then up to 16 hours a week or full time in June, July and August.

faq.q: Can I stay in the Netherlands after graduating?
faq.a: Yes. Within three years of graduating you can apply for a one-year orientation year, during which you may work without a work permit.
